utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we turn to the expert witness, there's one other administrative matter that I should deal with. It relates to the subpoena witness who was due to attend this week. You said you'd like the material in writing. I've checked with your Registrar, and the position is that the original report was filed and the material letter for this witness, which is a letter dated the 31st of December of 1999, is with your Registrar and will be copied and made available to you today, and I have no material beyond what is contained in that letter and in the earlier reports touching on that witness for you to act upon, and I'd ask you to act upon that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Registry has heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the expert witness, as I indicated yesterday, I'll let Ms. Somers deal with all matters of detail that may arise, although the thing is fully argued. I'd simply say these things: I think by way of general introduction, he was notified as a witness in the early witness list. His summary was served, and when his report was served, there was simply a notification that they desired to cross-examine him. It may well be, although we've responded to their skeleton argument in detail out of courtesy, it's really far too early. This is a proper case for the witness, who is plainly an expert and a much respected man, who wrote his book on ethnic cleansing in 1995, I think. He might well be a witness in other cases. It's far too early really to think about his expertise. It's probably a matter for him to come here and to be cross-examined, which is what would normally happen. The court will, I think, have already read his report and will know that his evidence in chief certainly wouldn't take very long, because it would be an question of adopting his reports, with some amplification. But that's all I would say by way of general introduction. Ms. Somers is available to deal with any queries should you want them to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's not a matter of detail; it's a matter of principle, on which I will be grateful for your assistance, speaking for myself, and that is to the extent to which those of us from common law backgrounds call or know as the ultimate issue rule. To what extent is this witness, in fact, drawing the inferences which are for us to draw? I have in mind a conclusion, which is referred to merely as an example. I'm looking, actually, at the Defence version, which is the one in colour, since that helps one lay their argument. If you have it at page 19. If you have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: "Based on the evidence adduced above, one can conclude that Kordic was the supreme HVO and HDZ official in Central Bosnia, and he displayed authority and power in both the traditionally military and civilian areas of authority and responsibility. This combination would have enabled him to control significant events. Further, it can be concluded that he acted in pursuit of concrete, previously planned policies. One can conclude that he encouraged a policy of confrontation with the Bosniak community, a pattern of activity in accord with his verbal statements, policy preparations and orders to subordinates. Given the range of his implied and actual powers, the reasonable conclusion, based on the available evidence, is that he would have been aware of such activities, and his degree of involvement and span of command responsibility extended over all significant armed elements and their major actions." Now, isn't that precisely what we have to determine, whether that is so or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those final conclusions are indeed issues that the Chamber will have to consider. They are, in reality, an overall conclusion, because the rest of his report leading up to that is expert conclusion supported generally by the footnotes. In fact, one of the characteristics of his report is that the first short part of the report is substantially conclusions; matters of pattern and similar topics are dealt with, supported by the footnote material to which complaint is made by the Defence. Then he comes to the overall conclusion at the end. Now, on whether you're allowed, these days, to have an expert giving an opinion on the final issue, we've addressed that argument or that topic in our skeleton, as the Chamber will recall, and the present position is that, of course, you are allowed, subject to certain specific exceptions in some jurisdictions -- I think it's at paragraph 9 -- you are allowed to have experts offering opinion based -- opinion on the final issue. The extent to which you do and the extent to which you're affected by that is ultimately a matter for the Chamber, but certainly that is now the position and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, you say that, but I question whether that really is the position. The fact that it happens is usually overlooked, I suspect, but I'm by no means satisfied that that is the normal position. The other thing is that -- does it help us? These are the matters that we have to decide. This is, in summary, your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The very last paragraph incorporates propositions that are indeed in part our case, but Your Honour will want to be looking at the supporting conclusions, which are elements within it and elements that go to support it, and they are also outside the -- they are the principle matters that are outside the experience of the Chamber and upon which expertise is vital and helpful. And in his survey of and marshalling of the material and then applying his analysis to reach the conclusions that precede the final conclusion, he is doing the work of an expert and not expressing final conclusions. And so the Chamber is left in this position, in our respectful submission, that the material leading up to the final conclusions is material that must be admitted and attended to, and the Chamber can decide for itself the extent to which it wishes to attend to those very last conclusions that Your Honour has read out to me. We would invite you to say that it is permissible and absolutely proper to have them in mind in much the same way as juries and, indeed, judges, trying cases alone, regularly now have opinions on the final issue in mind in either many or nearly all jurisdictions, always free to say to themselves, "But an expert is only a witness and he's a witness I can accept, accept in part, attend to to confirm my own provisional judgements, attend to to check where I find myself in disagreement with what the witness says, or to reject totally." And that, of course, is something easier done, it may be thought, by professional judges than by jurors, but in fact these days it is done by jurors. Accordingly, the answer to Your Honour's question is, yes, you may indeed attend and it would be proper to have before you those final conclusions, but it's the material that leads up to them that is perhaps much more important and much more valuable to you. If Your Honour would give me just one minute, please, because I want to ask just one question of one of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just reminding myself, because when you're looking for something in a document, you never find it. I said it's paragraph 9. It picks up at 10 on the question of the final issue, and then it's 15 and 16 that you'll find the citations for the final issue. Fundamentally, and unless Ms. Somers wants to draw to my attention anything else, it's all the work that precedes that that is of critical value to the Chamber. And if I may respectfully say so, to build on what I said at the beginning about this being, in a sense, quite a premature matter to raise at this stage and a matter properly raised with the witness when he's here, this is a case where the witness can attend, explain again his methodology, if that's in issue, and his expertise, and the Chamber can then decide how far through his report it wishes to hear from him in amplification or justification of his report. And if it chose to stop short at all or some of the last conclusions, that would be for the Chamber, but it's proper to be dealt with with the witness. The point is made by Ms. Somers, and I'm grateful to her for it, building on what I said about the potential of expert evidence on the final issue to assist triers of fact in all the ways I outlined; with that in mind, we've called the witness towards the end or very nearly at the end of the case so that, indeed, ways in which it matches and ways in which it doesn't match, either provisional judgements or other evidence, can be of maximum value to you. And that, indeed, is how an expert witness in most litigation is of value, because he typically comes at the end of a lot of other evidence and it's possible to use him as a check, one way or another, and especially when he's formed an opinion at an earlier stage and so can't be said to have been in any sense tailoring his evidence to what comes in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he gives evidence about the command responsibility, which is probably a mixed issue of fact and law, we would, in our judgement, presumably have to accept or reject it. But it doesn't matter what he says about command responsibility. That's our decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's your decision, but there is absolutely no prohibition against your attending to the expert opinion of someone else on the topic, and indeed throughout the evidence that you've been hearing, witnesses have effectively been giving evidence on that topic, either direct evidence, where they speak of some direct command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but this witness saw nothing. All he did was gather together the materials and come to an opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But he gathers together the material with expertise that is not available to us. This is a recognised and respected area of expertise to which he's devoted some part of his life, entirely neutrally gathering materials that aren't available to us in their broad range and knowing where to look, and that marks him out and it gives him a particular insight and a particular value. If I may respectfully say so, I think that the traditional view well known to common lawyers of concern about the expert expressing a final view has been disappearing for years. I think its first noted disappearance was probably in criminal cases with the issues of diminished responsibility, and for many years judges were anxious as to whether they could or should allow the psychiatrist to express the final view or not. That's now, I think, all clear. They can. And as that was changing in criminal cases, of course, the position was developing in civil cases as well and in other jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a particular form of expertise, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we could debate this -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, outside this business of general conclusions, the "ultimate issue question," quote/unquote, in the expert report and what you consider to be expertise: We call the witness to court; are there elements that we're not familiar with and which Mr. Cigar may bring to us through his expertise? That is what is important, if we leave aside the general conclusions, which are up to the Chamber, of course, and regarding which the opinion of this expert will not be of great assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The answer to Your Honour's question is, yes, that there are expert elements, as I've said, and indeed as we've attempted to set out in the argument we've presented. When I say "attempted," it's for this reason: We haven't slavishly gone to Professor Cigar to ask him to justify, through our words to you, that he is an expert and the way in which he is an expert, given that this issue is raised. That would be, perhaps, a somewhat unfortunate thing for us to do. We have established the areas of particular expertise, and they are set out in the skeleton. We've checked with him that it is appropriate for us to lay those matters before you, and he confirms that it is, in particular, the methodology of this particular expert and expertise. And it would, in our respectful submission, be quite wrong to exclude him on grounds that he isn't an expert without seeing him and attending to him. We say it's manifest that he is, not only by his access to material and, indeed, by his familiarity with matters of language and so on, but for all the other reasons that we've set out in the skeleton. It may be on this topic that Ms. Somers could be permitted a few words if it's troubling you, because she's looked at this with more detail and indeed she's been actively concerned in the preparation of this witness. But I must emphasise that this witness, although he appears now only in the Kordic case, may be the sort of witness who is particularly valuable or could be particularly valuable in these cases generally and this particular witness. Therefore, exclusion in advance and on paper would be, in our respectful submission, quite wrong. He must be given a chance to explain and to confirm what we say about the expertise he has. It's all -- not all too easy. It is easy sometimes to think that what one reads in an expert report is the mere collation of material. But indeed, and we know that in these trials, the collation of material by witnesses has been accepted as a proper form of evidence, but we don't, and we set out some reference to that in one of the much earlier cases. But we don't seem to rely on that heavily for the introduction of Professor Cigar's report, because we say he's a proper expert. Indeed he is an expert -- I don't think there's any doubt about that -- and a much respected one, whose material will be able to assist you, particularly in relation to patterns of consistency and behaviour broadly, sourcing material that simply isn't available to us. But can Ms. Somers deal with this particular part rather than her flood me with materials, and she can respond to Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Judge Robinson has a point and then we'll hear Ms. Somers briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, following upon the President's concern about the question of the final issue, this case is largely built on inferences. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It is significantly built on inferences, as I explained at the beginning. Indeed, at the beginning, never knowing how much direct evidence I would have, I made it quite plain that the case could be made out completely on inferences. In the event, as evidence has become available, there's more direct evidence than I forecast, but, yes, it is significantly more direct evidence of commands and so on. But, nevertheless, Your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And I think the question of command responsibility will be resolved substantially on the basis of inferences which the Tribunal will be able to draw from facts which have been testified to during the hearing. I think that the concern which is being expressed is that ultimately it is for the Tribunal to draw these inferences from the facts which we hear from the live witnesses and other testimony, and to what extent are we going to be helped by having a witness give his view as to that ultimate question. I think this is what concerns us, because ultimately that is a matter which we have to decide on the basis of the facts. He's not coming to testify as to any particular facts. He's coming to give his view as to the level of responsibility of a particular accused based on matters which have come to his knowledge through, admittedly, as you say, his expertise, on the basis of his expertise. But essentially that is a matter for us to decide, and to what extent are we going to be helped by it? For example, does it advance your case significantly more if you were able to -- if you, in your submissions, made a presentation arguing that you have presented sufficient facts which allow us to draw inferences as to command responsibility? Does it advance your case any more if you are to do that than to have this witness come and give his view as to the level of responsibility based on his expertise? I'm not sure myself that it advances your case significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, it's helpful to have your concerns so that I can address them. To some degree I'll be repeating what I said, but I can recast what I said in a way that I hope is helpful, and I'll give you an analogy as well. The answer to Your Honour's question is, yes, it indeed can help you and can help you significantly. And before I explain again why, can we underline one feature of the expert, which is sometimes overlooked when played out before Judges, is the adversarial system. The adversarial system is thought to involve selection and even strategic or tactical selection of material. It's not the case with this Prosecution, but it's often thought that's what happens. But even where there is any tactical or strategic selection of fact witnesses, and there hasn't been, even where there is, the witness comes as an independent body. Indeed, in England, and I expect elsewhere, there is a growing practice or requirement that the expert is actually the Court's expert. In some settings now, I know in England, the Court appoints an expert so that he comes absolutely neutrally. But that's only a reflection of what his position has always been. So when Your Honour says, "Is it not for us, the Judges, to draw the inferences from the raw facts?" the answer to that question is no. It is the Court's duty to draw the inferences or to make the findings from all the evidence. The evidence includes facts from which inferences are drawn, but it also includes relevant expertise in the form of opinion to which it can attend. And I now go back to the way I presented it at the beginning. Given that the material before the Court is facts in the form of evidence of facts and opinion, each of which we are entitled to lay before you, the Chamber then has the advantage, with its expert, of remembering that he is independent and not partial. And indeed in this case, as we know, he's published in various ways, well before this trial was started or maybe even conceived of; conceived of, I think. So he's a man whose views are of an integrity and long-standing integrity. So the Chamber is able then to attend to his expertise and expert opinion either to support, to check, or, indeed, as I've already said, to reject. There's a whole range of approaches to an expert. Is it helpful? Of course it is. Let us go back to -- I know a particular example, remote from the facts of this case but, nevertheless, the helpful one, for diminished responsibility. Here it may be that I'm speaking about a particular corner of United Kingdom-based law that will not be immediately known to His Honour Judge Bennouna, but if we go back to the example of diminished responsibility, the Chamber will know or recall that the diminished responsibility test, which I think has some reflection here as well, is a test little known to psychiatrists. It was a test put together by lawyers to serve whatever the then practical requirements of the legislature were, but it's a test which, nevertheless, incorporates psychiatric or quasi-psychiatric language. The test is one that you might think a layman or a juror could deal with himself, especially given the fact that the terminology doesn't really fit within the lexicon of the expert witness. And of course when the jury is asked the questions on diminished responsibility, it's asked to attend to all the evidence. But typically, if not in all cases, it is assisted by experts who come along and who look at the same material, and sometimes, of course, additional material in the form of psychiatric examinations. They build on the material, ordinary and expert, and they offer a conclusion. And the Judge says to the jury, "Accept it, reject it, deal with it as you will, but it's part of the evidence in the case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As the Presiding Judge says, that is a very particular case of legislation which sets out a particular definition of diminished responsibility. That's a very particular case. I don't think it derogates from the general principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In my respectful submission, it may be a particular case, but neither does it in any sense diminish the value of the approach, because the approach there is -- and one can think of lots of other examples where experts are typically led in evidence. I can think of plenty of other cases where tests have to be applied that might be in part legal, in part factual. One can think of, I suppose, almost endless examples, if one has the time, of factory accidents, matters of that sort, where there are tests to be applied either following on from rules and regulations or from Statute or, alternatively, under the common law, where there is a straightforward test to be applied and in respect of which an expert will be called, the expert opinion being part of the material upon which the Tribunal of fact and law decides but not being determinative of it. Those experts, typically, if not always these days, express a view on the final issue. Yes, there was a breach. Yes, there was negligence. Those issues are very close to issues of what was the nature of the command structure, very close. And in those cases, Judges do not deprive themselves of the advantage that such experts can give them. At the end of the exercise, they use the expert to check their provisional judgement, to bolster their judgement, or they reject it. But as professional Judges -- and these are, of course, in England, always cases tried by Judges alone -- they never have any difficulty in dealing with the material. And we would invite Your Honours to say that that is the approach that should be taken here, and that it does actually fall fairly and squarely within all of the other sorts of cases where experts are typically admitted. If that answers -- I hope it answers; at least it deals with His Honour Judge Robinson's questions. Then back to His Honour Judge Bennouna's question. It may be that Ms. Somers can help you with a few detailed matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The earlier expert witnesses were able to place for the chamber the facts and the times that are at issue in this indictment in a historical context and in a socio-cultural context. They stopped where their areas of expertise stopped. The context at which we must make sure is of record before this Chamber is the political and military context, which no one fact witness and indeed the other experts could not necessarily or could of necessity had to stop where their own natural limitations took over. Because Dr. Cigar is, through his professional expertise, able to, having collected, assess, synthesise and then conclude in a very neutral manner, roles of the different entities, all of which had events happening simultaneously, and because he looks at all the relationships of what's going on with the Serbs, what's going on with the Bosniaks, what is going on with the Croats, both within Croatia and within Bosnia at any given moment during the time span that this Chamber must bear in mind, it is extremely helpful to know what he can show you with the other relating events, because facts can be looked at differently depending on context. It is essential and must be presented to this Court the context of the conflict. It is exactly that type of examination which a political/military intelligence analyst, particularly with the background of Dr. Cigar, brings to this Court. The range of sources evidenced in the extensive footnotes, which are, of course, only a fraction of what this individual can bring to this Chamber, indicates probably the most unique referencing of the Croatian media, and indeed of the media of the former Yugoslavia, that has ever been brought before this Tribunal. It is critical to get an individual who is trained to know the value of sources to come before the Tribunal and get that information in. The ability to look at events over a long period of time and find patterns so as to be able to determine whether things were random or policy is essential to the indictment. Again, no one fact witness and perhaps even all fact witnesses, even taken together, because of their inherent limitations or the time during which they served in theatre, can bring this. The type of examination done by Dr. Cigar is specifically geared toward presenting the context with the fabric of what it means to be a political figure, what it means to be a military figure in that political and military structure. The issue has come up repeatedly, as Mr. Nice has indicated, and to have the correct person to address it is the thrust of our bringing Dr. Cigar in. Again, this conflict has presented facts and information which are susceptible of many interpretations, and all of us who have attempted to keep current and understand them still have limitations of either language or of just inability to scan or peruse the entire span of this vast field of information. As Mr. Nice rightly pointed out, it is Dr. Cigar's responsibility to go to these sources which address these issues that must be made part of the record. There is only a benefit to be derived. Rejection of certain findings is certainly within the sound discretion of the Chamber. But to complete and to show how things occurred, that they did not occur in a vacuum but are susceptible of a conclusion that there was policy, systematic, is absolutely critical, and this is the type of witness, clearly, who brings that information to the Chamber. If there are any specific questions, I would be very happy to address them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got nothing else to say at this stage, save to say that Mr. Guariglia reminds me that in paragraph 10 there is reference to the Tadic Trial Chamber and a witness who, I think, expressed a view on the final question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that's right. I know who that witness was --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- because she gave evidence in Kovacevic. She was a human rights historian or compiler of a report in Prijedor, and I think that is what she gave evidence about. I suspect that is what she gave evidence about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The objection to her evidence, the objection being overruled, was, indeed, as set out, that her opinions were on matters that it was the judgement of the Tribunal to supply, and the Tribunal made the conclusion that, nevertheless, her evidence should properly be admitted. I refer you to that for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me start by debunking a myth. First, Dr. Cigar is neither neutral nor an expert. In 1993, having opined that Mr. Kordic was an inveterate Muslim-hater, he doesn't come to this Court without his sense of bias about him, and indeed he started his project here for the Tribunal in 1996, having made that statement -- I believe it's on page 134 of his book -- public. Moreover, he offers no expertise that the Court doesn't already have. His PhD, or Doctor of Philosophy, is in Middle Eastern history and Arabic from the University of Oxford. His thesis was Mohammed L. Khadar's Nashr al Mathani, The Chronicles, which is a thesis about a Moroccan historian, born on 14 April 1712, who chronicled the struggle of various sultans. His undergraduate degree is in French. He has a Masters, of course, in international affairs and his M.S. in strategic intelligence is in Soviet Union areas studies. The long and short of all this is I do challenge what my opposition has said, and the bottom line is he is no more expert than the Bench. His graduate degrees versus our law training and our background are identical, and he clearly, and Your Honours clearly understand, he invades on your province. He is the fourth judge. He is the Prosecutor's closing argument, and he tries to make the case for the Prosecution. Indeed, I'm prepared, absent a showing of his bias, which will take 15 minutes, to waive cross-examination altogether if the Prosecution will waive its closing statement, because that is what Dr. Cigar is doing, and he's doing that in a fashion that is most insidious. I will pause only to mention that the colour-charted examples that we gave you clearly indicate what he does and doesn't do. His work is an analysis of press accounts, OTP witness statements, documents, videos and audiotapes, and other Tribunal cases, and the colour-coding, of course, in the skeleton argument is clear on that. It may not be as clear relative to the footnotes. Our colour-coding cites the various levels of hearsay. The reds show one, two, or three levels; greens, one, two, or three levels or evidence not in the record; and the blues and dark blues show other levels of unreliability, and that just may not be apparent. The Prosecution concedes, in its response and in its evidence or statements before the Tribunal today, as follows: The issues before the Court are complex and susceptible of obfuscation; page 4 of their pleading. Experts trained to look at often ambiguous facts, in light of their specialised knowledge and training, present their analysis to the Court. Paragraph 4. The exercise, in and of itself, benefits the Tribunal by looking at facts and events in a manner which otherwise may not, through no shortcomings of their own, be apparent. And then finally at page 5, paragraph 6, large amounts of evidence, which in one context may appear to indicate certain things and in another context brought to light by the expert's training and experience, may indicate other things. Now, what that all says is crystal clear. The evidence on the record before the Court --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The evidence before the Court is ambiguous. It is susceptible to many interpretations, but the only interpretations that count are yours. The Prosecution has decided to hire an expert to review not the record in this case but a shadow case. He has reviewed not the transcript which is available to him, he has not looked at the Defence cross-examination, nor has he heard the Defence side. He has instead looked at a variety of newspaper documents, things supplied to him by the Tribunal from witnesses, some of whom have appeared and some of whom have not, and he has made his conclusion. The worst part about his conclusion is he has made it -- and the Prosecution mercifully conceded this in its papers -- he has made his conclusion having decided the credibility and reliability of witness statements, reports in news journals, accepted some and rejected others. Indeed, on page 5 of their pleading, they concede Cigar's report contains not only news articles but a number of, quote, "open sources which have been analysed with due regard to their reliability." "Open sources" is apparently a word in the spy community of which he comes from. He means statements of witnesses. But the buzz words in this case is "with regard to their reliability." If I may be facetious, Judge Cigar has decided who is reliable and who isn't, taking that entirely from your hands, and presents to you his analysis of the shadow case which I suggest. Now, the Prosecution has suggested that we need Dr. Cigar because he provides information ordinarily outside the experience and knowledge of the judges of the facts. Because you are professional judges, experienced in international law, he adds nothing to the mix. Indeed, at the close of the evidence, although I do not know your process, I don't know whether you meet jointly or individually, but you have the evidence in front of you and you analyse it. You look at what you believe and what you don't believe, what was credible and what was not credible. You look at the circumstantial evidence, the direct evidence, and ultimately reach your conclusions. Dr. Cigar invades that province, because he takes the circumstantial case and he gives you his opinion on it. And the law, I believe, is clear that in order to sustain a conviction beyond a reasonable doubt, the Court, if it is to use circumstantial evidence, must conclude that those presumed facts must necessarily flow beyond a reasonable doubt to make the proven facts. Cigar's insidious report, analysing a case not before the Tribunal, essentially embarks on a process of undermining the sanctity of the Court with regard to that and injecting into the record, frankly, irrelevancy. His report is nothing more or less than the summary, if you will, already ruled on in the Tulica dossier. His report, with regard to the big picture, is the same as the investigator's report with regard to Tulica. And like the investigator's report with Tulica, he takes those witness statements at face value. He doesn't look at the cross-examination, and I've already mentioned that. Now, with regard to his method, and this becomes important -- I won't discurse on the law, but for two minutes I will discurse, if I may -- the method that he employs is unintelligible and it is conceded to be unintelligible by the opposition. Page 11, paragraph 15, Dr. Cigar brings a methodology of synthesis and deduction distinct to those who are expert in this discipline. Then they go on to say at page 9, paragraph 12, that this kind of discipline is taught with a high degree of commonality between courses. And at page 12, they concede, "The intelligence process cannot be reduced to a mathematical formula." In short, Dr. Cigar cannot tell you his method, except, "I look at it, I induce, I think through it, I compare, I contrast. We learn this in various schools. Indeed, there are various courses on this. I may even teach those courses." That's nothing that the Court can't do on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That, surely, is a matter for cross-examination, and if there are matters about the expertise, about the materials upon which the opinion is based, about the method with which the witness came to his conclusions, all that is the subject of cross-examination and ultimately a question of weight, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The answer, sir, is respectfully "no". The body of law on which Ms. Somers relies in her work and which I, to some degree, do is the respectful thought of our United States Supreme Court, where they talk about junk science. That's the Daubert opinion that Ms. Somers cites in her pleading. Daubert essentially said that the courts are the gatekeepers of that which should be kept from the triers of facts, the jury, and make preliminary screenings. I think that's a proper role. Everybody agreed with that. But to the extent that they do was then set forth in an opinion Ms. Somers ignored, and that is the March 1999 holding in Kumho Tire versus Carmichael, and the reason it's significant is because Justice Breyer of the Court, a noted Harvard law professor before he took the Bench, opined again on this very issue of what should be the kinds of things that the trier of facts hear. Now, of course, they make the dichotomy all the time between jury and judge, the judge screening appropriate expertise so the jury does or does not hear it, but in this particular case there is truly no difference, and in fact it goes even more, because you, as experienced professional judges, don't need this kind of help. So the modern view set out in the Kumho Tire is that the Court should be very reluctant to introduce junk science, expertise that doesn't show a methodology that is capable of articulation, repetition, analysis and peer review, and the role of the Court is to keep, essentially, evidence which looks tantalising, and may in fact be tantalising, out from the triers of fact unless it is reliable and probative, and in this particular case, since the method -- and that's what I'm focusing on -- is not apparent, it's just intelligence-gathering of open-source material, in short it's one man's opinion. Not only is it one man's opinion, Your Honours, but the reason why -- and ultimately I'm going to conclude on these two thoughts -- the reason why it's so insidious and should not be injected into the record is it's another death by a thousand cuts. We've had tons of military witnesses in this case. They've opined, based on on-the-ground experiences, about a variety of issues, but they haven't gone -- and some have gone so far on issues of command of control and responsibility to give their opinion. They were there. Appropriate. This is someone who wasn't there, who is taking evidence not before the Court, heard out of the presence of Mr. Kordic, and opining on what the conclusion is. And that's where I'd like to leave, not yet discussed, the confrontation rights, because Judge Cigar, and I am being facetious, Judge Cigar essentially is judge and trier of fact of witnesses not before the Tribunal, who you have not heard, and nor has Mr. Kordic had an opportunity to confront. He doesn't look at expert material, scholarly documents, treatises. He's not like the other experts in this case who at least made an attempt to read and review the scholarly literature on this subject. He's reviewed nothing but factual material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, are you saying any of these three things or all of them; first, that Mr. Cigar is not an expert? That would be a preliminary issue. That would raise a question of screening. If you are correct that he's not an expert, then we shouldn't hear him. Secondly, are you saying he's an expert but an expert who has gone about his business in a poor fashion? That's not a screening matter. That could be addressed in cross-examination. Thirdly, are you saying that the subject matter on which he is invited to testify is not one that is proper for expertise? And that brings to mind the issue raised initially by the Presiding Judge as to the ultimate issue. That would also be a screening matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Let me take them in order. The only reason I challenge in this form, at least, the qualifications of the expert is just because apparently, unless you speak up, you're deemed to have consented or admitted or waived. It is absolutely true that the issue of whether he is an expert or not is a screening matter. I only raise it because I didn't want to be held silent. The second question is his methodology. That is where the rubber meets the road in the United States, because if the expert's methodology is inappropriate, the jury or trier of fact will never hear it, and there are pre-trial hearings just like this. But the third and independent and separate point is, yes, when all is said and done, and I encourage you to read the report, it tells you how you should rule and, consequently, is of no assistance to the Chamber and isn't, therefore, a preliminary matter -- it isn't an assessment matter, because the report is going to be entered into evidence, it is his opinion, he will be briefly examined for a few minutes by the Prosecutor, and that's what the evidence will be. So I guess those are long answers to your questions. I hope I have answered them. But the reason we raise these things preliminarily is because, frankly, if this kind of process is allowed to go on, then we didn't need the first ten months of the trial. We could have just put Dr. Cigar on the stand. He's looked at a lot of literature out there, and you can rely on him, and that's the end of the case. If I hear right, Mr. Nice is essentially saying, "Consider the ramifications of this for other cases, because Dr. Cigar has been signed up for other cases." I don't think that's an appropriate argument. That's the floodgate argument, "You have to rule in our favour or the floodgates will open up or close." So Your Honours clearly -- and I was tempted not to use the 45 minutes allotted, but I resisted the temptation -- Your Honours clearly understand the nub of the issue is the invasion of Your Honours' particular province by a man who offers nothing more than you already have. Because I'm enormously sensitive, I like to think, by training and bias to the issues of confrontation, I raise that as well, because I think that's important. So that's all I have to say on that. Frankly, other than pointing out one more time that Dr. Cigar's report is hearsay upon hearsay upon hearsay, unreliability upon unreliability upon unreliability, and those things are set out perfectly adequately in our papers, I will say no more, unless the Court has any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stein.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I reply just on a couple of points, please. First of all, most of the points made by Mr. Stein really are matters for cross-examination. The challenges to expertise, the assertion of bias and matters are of that sort are not matters that the Chamber can deal with today. His credentials are set out in his report, and indeed further on page 11 of our argument. But insofar as they are raised today, it is, as I venture to say right at the beginning, simply too early. The complaint about sources and about the use of the word "reliability" doesn't reflect the fact that the vast majority of the sources to which Professor Cigar refers are quotations from newspaper articles, and it is, no doubt, with that in mind that he uses the word "reliability" in order to ensure that he diminishes material that may be less reliable than, for example, direct quotations from newspaper articles or television broadcasts and matters of that sort. On the question of whether he should have reviewed the evidence or not, well, two points emerge. Of course, if he sat here throughout the case reviewing the evidence, then there would be the complaint that he was invading your factual function. The second point: Insofar as the evidence given by witnesses whose statements he's looked at diverges -- normally it does or it doesn't; normally they simply confirm what they said, but insofar as there's divergence, that's a matter that can be dealt with by way of cross-examination. Yes. I think I've made the point that they are, for the most part, interviews. They're not articles. And the interviews are not only with -- they're with a range of people, including Boban and Kordic and other such people. Again, I'm not going to be able to argue his expertise for him. It's a matter that would require his being here. But I understand that expertise of this kind, these days, is some of the expertise that's relied on when decisions are made by armies and by politicians. It is reliable and it is the matter of expertise, and it's the only way you can have the fuller, wider context of this case, which may be of value to you. The suggestion that he should be brought at the beginning is again unfortunate. It's for the very reason that he's here as an assistance and a check but not to substitute that he has been brought at the end. I have to say we reject the unhappy and somewhat extravagant criticisms of the witness, but in any event, were they to be as well-founded as Mr. Stein would like you to believe they are, they can be dealt with by him in cross-examination. So coming back to His Honour Judge Robinson's three queries as to whether by distinguishing between screening matters and other matters the evidence should be excluded, it's our respectful submission that there's absolutely no grounds for exclusion, because it's either a preliminary matter expertise that's for the witness to deal with, and it can't be dealt with on paper; it's either a question of complaining about the deployment of his expertise, again, as I think His Honour was raising as a possibility a matter for cross-examination and not a matter of preliminary nature. And the other issue of real screening doesn't arise, because this witness gives evidence of opinion on the steps towards the final conclusions and the final conclusions, all of which are properly admissible. I don't think I need go any further than that. I repeat again that the evidence wouldn't take very long certainly in chief, and that the Chamber could itself -- I see Mr. Stein wants to say something else, but before he does, I'm not encouraging the Chamber to do this, but Chamber's ability to regulate its proceedings means that it is not the case of the witness coming in and I or Ms. Somers saying, "Is this your report?" and that standing as the evidence, as the Chamber can itself say to what degree, at that stage, it's going to accept all of the report as evidence. And it may be the case that the Chamber would, given some of the concerns it's expressed this morning, invite us, if the evidence is led, to deal with particular topics before it then says, "Well, we will incorporate those paragraphs into the evidence." And that would be an exercise of discretion by the Chamber well within its powers, because we don't suggest that any right we have to call relevant evidence is a right to impose on the Chamber all of that evidence. The Chamber has its own powers. I have one more note. Let me see what it says. 94 bis does not contemplate the exclusion. It only contemplates cross-examination. We've made that point in the skeleton argument, and I said we don't rely on it heavily, but it's not lacking in importance. The contemplation is that experts will be led if they're relevant. This one is an expert, this one can show he is, and that there will be cross-examination. That's all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, we usually don't allow continued debate. You've had your go.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: They went first. I thought -- I have two minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the order is -- they went first, and they have the right of reply. You don't have one. We've heard enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've considered this matter. We do have in mind Rule 94 bis, of course, which contemplates a procedure in relation to expert evidence. However, it doesn't affect the Trial Chamber's power to exclude evidence under Rule 89 or, as in this case, 89(C), which allows the Chamber to admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. Much of the complaint made by the Defence about this witness is matter which is susceptible to cross-examination and is a question of weight. However, they raise a fundamental point, which is that what this witness effectively is doing is to provide evidence or provide opinion, more accurately, upon the very matters upon which this Trial Chamber is going to have to rule, and that, as they correctly point out, invades the right, power, and duty of the Trial Chamber to rule upon the issue. And matters have been raised in argument about that, and I refer, in particular, to the conclusions about command responsibility. But the evidence of the witness which has been put forward doesn't stop there. It is littered, if I may say, with examples of conclusions, drawing inferences, drawing conclusions, which it is the duty of this Trial Chamber to consider and to draw if appropriate or to reject. It's correctly pointed out that the witness hasn't heard the evidence. We have, and we have to decide the case. It's not a matter for him to decide. It may be that in certain circumstances experts are now permitted in jurisdictions, certain jurisdictions, to give evidence about the ultimate issue, but we don't think that this is such a case. We also don't think, and this is a matter where Rule 89(C) comes into play, that his evidence is going to assist us very much. 89(C) says we may admit any relevant material which it deems to have probative value. Because it's dealing with the matters which we have to deal with ultimately, drawing the conclusions and inferences which we have to draw, we think that it does not assist and is, therefore, not of probative value. We have in mind, of course, all of the evidence which we've heard over the last ten months in so deciding. Accordingly, we shall exclude the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases. The next witness is producing the video. I have yet to speak to him. He wasn't around yesterday afternoon. I believe the video is here and I believe he's outside. I don't know if I could presume to suggest a short break now, the overall consequence of which might be that we will not only meet the 12.30 deadline but possibly even finish before it, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's about the right time to take the break. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The witness is here. If you would take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd like to take a seat, Mr. Capelle. Examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Capelle, I think you were a Lieutenant-Colonel in the French Army. You were in Bosnia for several years at the time of the conflict, and you are more recently working for the OTP as a military analyst; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us a little bit about the time in Bosnia so that you can explain how well you would have known the area. How many years were you there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: The first time I worked in Bosnia in 1991 with the European committee as a monitor. Then I returned in 1992 with the first mandate of UNPROFOR, and I was with the headquarters in Sarajevo, and I was Assistant Officer for the UNPROFOR. Then I returned in 1993, and I was military observer in Sarajevo. In 1994 I became the Liaison Officer with the HVO in Posusje. And in late 1994 I was posted to the headquarters in Zagreb as the Intelligence Officer with the UNPROFOR, and I was with them until 1995. In 1995, I came back to the Tribunal as the military analyst, and then I went for a short time to Bosnia, and I stayed there once again for about one year and a half.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The video that we're going to be looking at was made on what day?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: This video was made on the 25th of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were involved in preparing the mission in which the video was made, but you didn't, in the event, travel in the helicopter while the video was being taken?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Correct. I prepared that mission, which had two stages. First, taking recordings on the ground through the villages, and the second stage was the video which I prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A request that the witness slows down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I know that the witness is indeed bilingual. He's speaking French for various reasons. He may find that he speaks at the speed more helpful if he speaks in English. I expect he'll speak in both languages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But whatever it is, can you do it fairly slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Choose whichever language you like, but slowly.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... we're going to cover a lot of territory very quickly. I can tell the Chamber that the video, first of all, goes up the Lasva Valley and then comes back again. It may not be necessary to go beyond the first part of the trip, which will be a little under an hour, I think. I've raised with my learned friends whether it would be helpful, subject to the Court's view, for them to be allowed simply to ask that the video be stopped at any points where they want to make points, if that happens, rather than for the whole thing to be rerun again for a second time. This may or may not create difficulties for those taking notes; I don't know. But subject to all those problems, I would invite that as a possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Stein and Mr. Kovacic, I mean that seems a sensible course, unless you particularly want to do it in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: My sense is there may come a time, but I doubt it, that we stop the video. At the end, however, either through cross-examination or a statement, we would like to address the Court as to, frankly, what's not on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if there is some point on the video where either of you want to raise a point or any counsel wants to raise a point, it might be sensible to get it stopped then and there and we can look at whatever it is that you want to be pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Very good, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the witness will himself ask that the tape be stopped from time to time just to explain where we are, what we are doing. I think the Chamber will, in particular, probably want to have a look at Kaonik. Kaonik is difficult to see from the road, but it is possible to see it through the trees on the video. If there's any view of the mountain road, and Colonel Capelle thinks that there is, it might be worth looking at that, because that is a different type of terrain from the rest of the valley, which is low and somewhat intimate. There may be other places at which the witness will suggest we stop the video. Subject to that, may the video, which is Exhibit 2799, be played, and may I, with the Court's leave, be seated except when I have to stand, as it were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: The video begins with a view of the village of Tulica, which is 11 kilometres to the south-east of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Without stopping the video, can the witness, perhaps at a suitable time, select a place to stop and point out where we see destroyed roofs or destroyed buildings so that we can thereafter recognise them more easily for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes. We're reaching the area of destruction of Tulica. One characteristic is that most roofs have disappeared, which below them sometimes houses are intact. In parts of the video, one can see the areas which are somewhat blackened, as houses which have been set on fire, even though the roofs are still in place. One sees here that the majority of roofs have disappeared from the houses. The helicopter is now flying over a zone which was all criss-crossed with trenches in the area of Tulica. This now appears quite clearly on the screen. One can also see that there are several lines of trenches, and that is what one finds on the ground all the time, more than one line of trenches. The helicopter has now turned towards Kiseljak, that is, north-west, and is reaching the area of Grahovci and Han Ploca. This village is along a road which climbs up the hill to the crest which dominates the road Kiseljak-Sarajevo. We see the houses still have their roofs, but most of them are destroyed. Here we again see this net of trenches, and down there is the village Han Ploca, Grahovci. We are reaching the village of Rotilj, which is to the north -- that is, to the west of Kiseljak to south-west of Kiseljak, south-west of Kiseljak some two kilometres. Now you can see that the windows have mostly disappeared from the houses, which is a sign, and then a number of destroyed houses. Some of these houses do not have roofs anymore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without stopping the video, when you see an example of roofs that can be distinguished sometimes between Muslim and Croat roofs, will you just draw that to the Chamber's attention, please.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that. Now we have reached Kiseljak, and we see in the centre what was the Kiseljak mosque. Its minaret has disappeared. The mosque was to the north of that town, near the road between Kiseljak and Busovaca. Now we're flying over the height of Kiseljak, and it's reaching the HVO barracks in Kiseljak. These barracks are to the south-west of the town and along the route between Kiseljak and Kresevo. The helicopter is now turning west of Kiseljak, and this is the village of Visnjica, about three and a half kilometres west of the town. The helicopter follows the road then which leads to Visnjica. Could you -- stop, please, the film. Could you stop the film? Now, on the hills beyond, one can see that there are no more windows, and all these houses are gutted out. And the majority of the houses which were on the crest up here are destroyed. You can proceed with the film. Yes, you can proceed with the film. We are now arriving at Visnjica, which I should say is in a valley, and here almost all of the houses were destroyed. Now we see that these houses are along the road, and we're passing over the mosque in Visnjica. We are reaching the exit from the village of Visnjica, and the helicopter will now fly over the village. The houses that you see here were destroyed, and in 1996 nobody lived there, and even the houses which had the roofs on. Here we are turning. We see the mosque now. It will appear on your right. The helicopter now arrived at Polje Visnjica, which is along the Kiseljak-Busovaca main road. There are destroyed houses. There are also intact houses there in which the Croat population in the Kiseljak region resides. Would you stop the film, please? Could you stop the tape? Now you can see, to the right and above, and it is relatively clear -- will you please stop the tape? Could we go slightly back, please? We missed that. You can see here roofless houses, and we can see very clearly some houses which do have roofs but the interior of which has been burned or otherwise destroyed. Yes, I think we passed those pictures. Yes, we can move on. Now we are following the road between Kiseljak-Busovaca, passing over Hercezi Duhri, flying over the mosque. And here we are still in the same area near Visnjica and about two or three kilometres away from Kiseljak. We are still in the same area. One can see very clearly the mosque in the centre or, rather, to the left and to the centre. Then we cross the road Kiseljak-Busovaca and turn to the north-east in the direction of Gomionica, and indeed the destruction here is much more evident. Almost all of the houses are without roofs. Behrici is a village adjacent to Gomionica. These villages are on the slope facing the Kiseljak-Busovaca road. We are making a circle and turning towards Gomionica. Would you stop there? Could you stop the tape, please? Here again -- yes, thank you. Once again, we see a group of houses which were all destroyed, all of them. One sees, for instance, houses to the right and closer to us that still have roofs, but one can see that the interior of all those houses was destroyed, and the same holds true of the houses which are behind those in the front. You can move on. We are still flying over Gomionica. We have made a circle, in fact. We are now going towards Svinjarevo, a little bit to the north of Gomionica. We are still following the Kiseljak-to-Busovaca road. This is Svinjarevo that I spoke about a moment ago, a village adjoining Behrici and Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is this a valley that we're going up?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed we're going up a valley. The villages that we're going to see are on the slopes of that valley, on the slopes of the hills. And I think that the river flowing through that valley is the Mlava River. We're still not in the Lasva Valley. We're south of Busovaca, the Mlava Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is it sometimes referred to as the Kiseljak Valley, or is that somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: There are several valleys around Kiseljak, and I don't think this can be called the Kiseljak Valley. But the axis to the north of Kiseljak, going towards Busovaca, goes along a valley up to the zone where we are now. So we are in a valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we go on, please.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Could you stop the camera. What appears more clearly now on the screen is the mosque on Svinjarevo and the roof. However, the quality of the picture doesn't allow to us see the details, but the roof has been partially destroyed. And as in the case of most mosques that we saw in the area, the minaret has been destroyed by explosives. It has been mined. We can play the tape now.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Can we stop the tape, please. What we see on the screen now is the helicopter is leaving the area of Svinjarevo and we are also leaving the zone of Kiseljak. Actually, you had a question regarding this valley. Yes, we went along a valley, and we saw a certain number of villages situated on one and other side of that valley going from Kiseljak. We saw those villages up to Svinjarevo, which are to the right and left of the road that follows the valley, and we are now going to another area, the area of Busovaca. These areas were separated by a corridor controlled by the Bosniak forces during the conflict. So the next pictures will be of villages to the south of Busovaca. There's an entire area known as the Kacuni corridor, which will be shown on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: The first village we're going to see now to the south of Busovaca is the village of Dosnici [phoen], situated to the south-east of Busovaca. We're still in Svinjarevo. We can see the trenches now on the high ground above Svinjarevo. Here again we have houses with roofs, but it is quite clear that the houses have been destroyed nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you remember to comment on the shape of the roofs when you find an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes. The majority of Muslim houses had roofs with four slopes, as you can see, as opposed to houses that we're going to see in Croatian villages. Most Muslim houses have roofs with four slopes. Now we are in the area of Busovaca already, and we are two or three kilometres south of Busovaca. This area is on the hills overlooking the Busovaca-to-Kiseljak road. The area here is covered and, unfortunately, many of the pictures taken from the helicopter does not fully display the relief of the terrain. Here the destruction is also very clear, even when there are parts of roofs remaining, as we see on the screen now. We're still in the same area; that is, flying over the hills south of Busovaca. We have now reached the Draga camp to the south of Busovaca, a camp located in a narrow valley, just before the entrance to the town. And we are now above the Busovaca-to-Kiseljak road. To the left is Kiseljak, to the right is Busovaca. The building there is a building occupied by HVO forces. We are leaving the camp and heading towards Busovaca. We're flying over the town of Busovaca. Here too we can see some destruction of houses, some houses without roofs, when that is very clear, but others with roofs, when the interior has been destroyed. The destruction we have just seen were on the periphery of the town, to the north, on the outskirts of the town. Here is an indication of the Busovaca mosque that we're going to see on the screen. Now we're overflying the northern suburbs of the town. A few kilometres from Busovaca is Kaonik, the Kaonik camp, and you can notice that the buildings of this camp are surrounded by trees, and it is virtually impossible to see it. We see the road to the left, and it is almost impossible to see the buildings of Kaonik camp, which is concealed by the vegetation and which is on a hill. We're only two kilometres -- two and a half kilometres from Busovaca. We're still flying over the buildings of the camp. The helicopter is now leaving Kaonik camp and is heading to the west, to the villages of Strane and Merdani. These villages are in the Lasva Valley. We're passing Strane now, where the destruction is quite evident. We are two or three kilometres to the west of Kaonik camp and close to the road of the Vitez-Kakanj or Vitez-Zenica road. The helicopter is now going to cross the Lasva Valley to go to the north of the valley and fly over the villages of Putis, Jelinak, and Loncari. That's where we are now. To the left you can see the hills which are part of the Kuber range. When we visited these villages, they were already in the process of reconstruction. As you will be able to see, some of the roofs are completely new. And now we see that this area is far more open than the area around Busovaca. Here we see on the screen that some of the roofs are new and a great deal of damage is evident. We're in the same area to the south of the Kuber range, and we're flying over now Gravrino Kuce. We're only some eight kilometres away from Vitez, which is a maximum ten-minute drive from Vitez. "The mosque at Putis" is written on the screen, but you can't see it at all. A large number of houses in Putis were already repaired or in the process of repair when we visited. On the screen, it says that the area we are flying over is not really known. In fact, it could be the hamlet of Bakiye, which is situated between Loncari and Putis at the top of a hill. We are still in the same area south of the Kuber range, a very important area, from the strategic point of view, for the freedom of action along the Busovaca-Vitez route, and we're going to leave that area now to approach Vitez and fly over Nadioci and Ahmici. We have now arrived in Nadioci in the Lasva Valley, and we are flying over the Vitez-Busovaca road. We're now approaching the location of a bungalow, what was called the Bungalow in Nadioci. Here almost all of the houses in Nadioci were destroyed. So the helicopter is now flying over Nadioci hills and is approaching Ahmici, and here again this village is against the range which -- mountain range or, rather, the hill range which is very important, because it controls the road. So now we are overflying the location of the Bungalow. We passed it by, and it was destroyed meanwhile. We are now coming to Ahmici from the south. We see the Vitez-Busovaca road in front of us now, and one can distinguish in the centre the road which leads to Ahmici. We are now on the other side of the road and overflying Ahmici. We are overflying the part which is the closest to the Vitez-Busovaca road, and almost all the houses -- practically all the houses here were destroyed. There are only a few intact houses, and these are inhabited by Croats. Now we can see in the centre of the screen the mosque in the lower part of Nezirovici. It disappears down on the monitor, but we shall see it now in the centre. Now we are going up Ahmici and then moving to the Upper Ahmici. Here we are above Ahmici, in the upper part of Ahmici. And here, because the roofs are there, one might think that the houses are intact, but they are, nevertheless, destroyed. I'm referring to the houses that we can see on the screen. We are still in the upper part of the village of Ahmici, and this is the mosque in Upper Ahmici. This is the mosque in Lower Ahmici. Its minaret was broken, and it fell on the roof of the mosque. We see the Vitez-Busovaca road. Now the helicopter turns, and we see -- at the bottom, we see that we are now coming to Vitez, about five minutes from the town. Now we are flying along the road and coming to Santici, which adjoins the village of Ahmici as one approaches Vitez, and we can see the range which dominates the valley and then Kuber in the background. Here we are about two and a half kilometres from Vitez. Now we have reached the area of Pirici, and we see the roofs which had been repaired. It is quite clear on the house which has just disappeared from the screen. That roof had been rebuilt. And it says here all the area that one can see from the helicopter, that we saw, and the area that we are flying over, that is, the whole area that we saw formally. And now all this area is strewn with mines, so that one could not move on foot very much and enter all the villages. We are still flying over the north part of the Vitez-Busovaca road, and this is still the area of Pirici. But this time we're flying near the trenches. It was impossible to go to this high ground at the time because of the mines. We are now in the upper part of Sivrino Selo, and we are approaching, slowly, Vitez. Sivrino Selo, as I mentioned, is just north of Dubravica in the outskirts of Vitez, a suburb of Vitez. The helicopter has now reached Stari Vitez and is about to fly over the chemical plant. Here we are, the first building. So this is the chemical plant making explosives, and it went on working for the duration of the conflict. We're now approaching Gacice, which is to the west of Vitez, near the chemical plant, and moving on to Veceriska, also in the vicinity of Vitez. We are now two kilometres from Vitez. We can see here that the hills above the factory, all this area, the buildings there and in Gacice were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please remember, if you get a sighting of the mountain road to Zenica, to stop the video and point it out to us.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: At the moment, we are not in the area of that road. We are to the south/south-west of Vitez now, and the road that you are talking about is to the north/north-west. We are still over the area of Gacice, close to the chemical plant, and still west of Vitez. In point of fact, one can see the plant on the left-hand side of the screen. We are still in Gacice, but now this is a close-up and this is the north view. Now we are coming into Vitez or, rather, Stari Vitez, approaching Stari Vitez. We are still overflying the plant. Now the helicopter heads south of Vitez to the area of Kruscica, but we are still close to the plant; that is, still near Veceriska and Gacice. As a matter of fact, this is Veceriska that we can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've seen quite a lot of the chemical works. Maybe we can speed it up.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes. We are about to arrive in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we're probably approaching the time when the helicopter returns, and at that point we can stop the video. It's possible we can accelerate it and go fast-forward if the Chamber has had enough of this particular passage.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: There are several interesting images, perhaps, and these are of the quarry which is to the north-west, where there was the civilian headquarters of the HVO, and also some interesting images of Kruscica. But we are in Stari Vitez, and here again we can get an idea of the destruction of Stari Vitez. A large number of these houses have already been repaired, or some are being repaired. So we -- the helicopter is overflying Stari Vitez and the area where the victims of Ahmici were buried. We are overflying the road which leaves Vitez; that is, the road leading north of Vitez, leading to Travnik. We enter Vitez from north. To the right of the screen, we can see Vitez Hotel and the HVO headquarters. Excuse me. On the left-hand side of the screen, we see the Vitez Hotel, on the left-hand side. And up in the upper part to the right is the cinema. It had disappeared from the screen, but we are now moving to the southern part of Vitez. And there is some buildings destroyed, which are gradually disappearing from the screen. Now the helicopter is making a circle and turning back to the northern part of the town. We shall shortly see the Vitez school, and I believe we will see the cinema once again. Here we are there. The cultural centre was to the left. We can't see it anymore. But to the left at the top of the screen we see the school, and it reappears on the screen on the left-hand side. So we see the distance from the centre of the city and the Hotel Vitez -- rather, the headquarters. It is only about a hundred metres. This building is a municipal hall of Vitez; that is, the administrative centre. If you could now move fast-forward. Can you speed it up, please? Yes, you can slow it down now. You can slow it down now. We are reaching Kruscica, which is to the south of Vitez. This was the zone controlled by Muslims during the conflict. You can fast forward now, please, again, because the helicopter is about to once again fly over the northern part of Vitez and the quarry in the north of Vitez. So the helicopter goes back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have we reached the place where the helicopter is about to return?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Not yet. It will be after we overfly the quarry, and I think we're about to reach it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Unless there's anything in the remaining film that you think we should look at, we'll perhaps terminate it there.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes. We're once again flying over the area that we saw, and the only different thing which one can see here is the quarry before, and it may be interesting, but otherwise we do not see here any footage of destruction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll just have a look at the quarry, because it does feature in the evidence, if it doesn't take us too long to get there. We didn't find anything along the mountain road, but we can see in general the size of the mountains to the north of Vitez. As we were flying over Busovaca, I don't know if you're aware of the road to Tisovac, but it was barely visible, although the wooded area in which it passes could be seen.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Now it crosses to Grbavica, and we are about to come to the quarry. We're about to -- we can see Grbavica, the village, which was destroyed, on the hill which is now disappearing to the right. We see destroyed houses. Now we can see the quarry. Slow down, please. We're some three kilometres, three and a half to the north of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The "Nora" referred to on the screen refers to what?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: It is an HVO gun, an HVO cannon, and it was in this area, positioned in this area, in the quarry. As one comes down from the quarry, there is an area which was quite -- an area where it was quite possible and easy to position various artillery pieces. Now we're in the quarry. We see what it looks like now, and that is rather surrounded and, therefore, it offered good protection for whatever materiel was there. And now we're leaving the quarry. I don't know if you want to follow to the end of the film. We're going back to Vitez. We have the Lasva Valley in front of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's been ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It seems to have been edited, making the decision for the witness. So there we are. Nothing else I want to ask of Colonel Capelle. I'm grateful to him for his commentary as we've been going along. Cross-examined by Mr. Naumovski:

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have a few questions for you, Witness, of a principal nature. My name is Mitko Naumovski. I'm Defence attorney from Zagreb, and I am one of the lawyers defending Mr. Kordic. Tell me, please, how long you spent in the Central Bosnia area, if you can. Approximately.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: I did not live in Central Bosnia, but I passed through the area on several occasions. I had to pass through to go to the headquarters in Kiseljak, to travel between Sarajevo and Kiseljak, to go to Gornji Vakuf, to travel between Gornji Vakuf and Vitez, to travel between Posusje, Gornji Vakuf, Vitez, Zepce. So so I went through this area on a number of occasions quite frequently, but I never actually stayed in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you know -- were we -- were you told which municipalities belonged to the area of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't take notes about it. Yes. I was told about the municipalities of Central Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, sir, you drew up the plan for the filming but were not present when the filming was done, but you did make a plan for that, you did plan it all.

utterances.speaker: JEAN PIERRE CAPELLE
utterances.text: For this mission I was given a list of villages which the investigative team should visit. The time given to us was quite short, so we had to do it in logical manner, to identify the co-ordinates which would allow the people accompanying us, that is the SFOR people, to work in convenient conditions with us, and I acted as more of a topographer then than as an historian or geographer, as you seem to indicate.
